verses.text: Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.
He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.
Their father gave them great gifts of silver, of gold, and of precious things, with fortified cities in Judah; but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.
Now when Jehoram had risen up over the kingdom of his father, and had strengthened himself, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did Ahab’s house; for he had Ahab’s daughter as his wife. He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight.
However Yahweh would not destroy David’s house, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and as he promised to give a lamp to him and to his children always.
In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah, and made a king over themselves.
Then Jehoram went there with his captains and all his chariots with him. He rose up by night and struck the Edomites who surrounded him, along with the captains of the chariots.
So Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah to this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time from under his hand, because he had forsaken Yahweh, the God of his fathers.
Moreover he made high places in the mountains of Judah, and made the inhabitants of Jerusalem play the prostitute, and led Judah astray.

A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, “Yahweh, the God of David your father, says, ‘Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, nor in the ways of Asa king of Judah,

but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and have made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to play the prostitute like Ahab’s house did, and also have slain your brothers of your father’s house, who were better than yourself,
behold, Yahweh will strike your people with a great plague, including your children, your wives, and all your posessions;
and you will have great sickness with a disease of your bowels, until your bowels fall out by reason of the sickness, day by day.’”
Yahweh stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines, and of the Arabians who are beside the Ethiopians;

and they came up against Judah, broke into it, and carried away all the posessions that were found in the king’s house, including his sons and his wives; so that there was no son left him, except Jehoahaz, the youngest of his sons.
After all this Yahweh struck him in his bowels with an incurable disease.
In process of time, at the end of two years, his bowels fell out by reason of his sickness, and he died of severe diseases. His people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers.
He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years. He departed without being missed; and they buried him in David’s city, but not in the tombs of the kings.

footnotes.content: Jehoshaphat's long, faithful reign ends as it must—in David's city, the very place where the dynasty began. His son Jehoram inherits not just the throne but all his father's prayers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five brothers, each carrying their father's name in some form—Azariah means 'God helps,' and they should have helped one another. Instead, they'll soon learn what it means to stand alone against a crowned brother.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A father's love is generous to all his children, yet the kingdom goes to one. Jehoram receives the highest gift and the hardest test—and he will choose poorly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Power can corrupt a heart so quickly. Jehoram sees his brothers as threats the moment he takes the throne, forgetting that his father's strength came from walking with the Lord, not from cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirty-two years old—still young enough to learn, still young enough to change. Eight years ahead of him, and not one prayer for wisdom marks this beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A marriage brings him into Ahab's household—and Ahab's gods. How many times have we seen compromise slip in through affection, small at first, then poisoning everything?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is mercy that Jehoram does not yet see: God keeps His promise to David even when the son turns away. The lamp still burns, the house still stands—not because Jehoram deserves it, but because the Father's word is sure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The moment you turn from the Lord is the moment His protection begins to slip away. Edom sees a weakened kingdom and takes its chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By night he strikes—there is still some fight in him, some echo of his father's courage. Yet even a military victory cannot hold what a soul has already lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One falls; another rises. As Jehoram drifts from the God of his fathers, the lands slip from his grip. It is a mercy disguised as loss—the Lord shaking his throne to wake him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: High places built in the mountains—altars to false gods, and his own people led to stumble. A king's sin never stays small; it spreads like bitter fruit to all who look to him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah the prophet, long moved from the world of Ahab's Phoenicia, sends a letter—the Lord still reaches across the distance to call His wayward son home, using even an old prophet's pen to write mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The indictment is sharp: not just his own wrong, but his brothers' blood on his hands. Yet even now, if he repented, the Lord would hear. Jehoram does not turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The threat comes with a terrible scope—his people, his children, his wives. Sin that clings to a leader brings suffering to all he loves. This is the weight of the crown when worn in rebellion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The specific plague—bowels failing day by day—strips away dignity with pain. The Lord meets stubborn pride with a judgment that cannot be hidden or denied.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philistines from the west, Arabians from the south—enemies gather when the Lord withdraws His shield. No throne is truly secure without His hand beneath it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They take everything—even his sons and wives, symbols of his dynasty and hope. Only the youngest remains, Jehoahaz, a boy who will himself face a truncated reign. How many generations suffer for one man's turning away?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's hand strikes directly now—no plague from enemies, but from His own judgment. There is loneliness in knowing that what falls upon you comes from the One who gave you breath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two years of decline, and then the end—the very word Elijah spoke comes to pass. He dies without honor, without the fire lit for him as for his fathers. This is what becoming is left behind looks like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this epitaph: a man reigned, then vanished—'without being missed.' How will we be remembered? What do we leave behind when we turn from the light?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
